where: Section 2 selection order, Section 3 policy paragraph, Quiz Q7
problem: MED is treated as a general tie-breaker that can be compared across different neighbouring ASes. By default BGP compares MED only among routes received from the same neighbouring AS; MED is also non-transitive. Q7 compares MED 50 from ISP A with MED 80 from ISP B and says 50 wins, and Section 3 says MED can steer inbound traffic across two ISPs. Both are wrong or misleading under standard BGP.
fix: Add the same-neighbour caveat wherever MED is described. In Q7, either make both routes come from the same ISP (then MED 50 wins) or state that with different ISPs MED is ignored unless always-compare-med is configured and later attributes decide. In Section 3, say MED can influence inbound traffic for multiple links to the same neighbouring AS; for two different ISPs use AS_PATH prepending or other policy.

problem: The node AS10 is labelled with note 'origin'. In BGP the origin AS is the last AS in AS_PATH (AS30 or AS60 in this example); AS10 is the local/receiving AS where the route decision is made. The figure also marks AS30 and AS60 both as 'prefix' for the same /24 without explaining that this means multi-origin.
fix: Change AS10's note to 'local AS' or 'decision point'. Keep 'origin/prefix' on AS30 and AS60 only if you explicitly say the same prefix is originated by two ASes (multi-origin/anycast); otherwise use one origin AS.

problem: 'nearest AS first' is ambiguous. A student may read it as nearest to the origin AS. BGP puts the most recently added AS, closest to the receiving AS, first, and the origin AS last.
fix: Write 'from the AS closest to the receiver (most recently added) to the origin AS' and in Q1 'most recently added AS first, origin AS last'.
